Plessy v. Ferguson. In 1896, Homer Plessy boarded a whites-only railroad car in New Orleans to challenge the constitutionality of Louisiana's segregation law. He was one-eighth Black, and the state arrested him. The Supreme Court voted 7 to 1 to uphold the law's constitutionality.

Justice Henry Brown wrote that segregation was constitutional if facilities were separate but equal. That phrase became the foundation for systematic racial apartheid in the South for the next sixty years. Brown reasoned that the 14th Amendment guaranteed political equality but not social equality, allowing states wide latitude to classify citizens by race. The Court ignored that the separate facilities were almost never actually equal in practice.

Justice John Harlan dissented memorably. He argued the Constitution is color-blind and that the ruling would embolden discrimination. He was right. Plessy provided legal cover for widespread segregation across schools, transit, public accommodations, housing, and voting. The doctrine justified the entire Jim Crow regime.

In 1954, fifty-eight years after Plessy, the Supreme Court finally overturned it in Brown v. Board of Education. Brown explicitly declared that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal, rejecting the very foundation Plessy had laid. But between 1896 and 1954, one flawed decision had enabled a system of racial oppression affecting millions of lives.
